title: Stage Capabilities: Install Digital Certificate
summary: Adversaries install TLS certificates on infrastructure they control so that command and control traffic is encrypted and credential harvesting pages appear trustworthy. A certificate binds a public key to a host name and carries a signature from a certificate authority, so any client that trusts that signer will complete an encrypted session without complaint. Attackers either obtain a publicly trusted certificate through ordinary, largely automated registration flows, or generate a self signed one on the server itself. A trusted certificate makes the traffic indistinguishable from normal secure web browsing at the network layer, which defeats simplistic content inspection and lets a padlock appear in the address bar. Defenders catch this through certificate transparency logs, which record every publicly trusted certificate issued for a name, and through monitoring for newly registered domains that host login forms. Self signed certificates remain a useful signal, because most clients still warn or log an error when they meet one.

beginner.definition: A digital certificate is a small file that proves a server's identity on the internet. It lets two computers talk in private using encryption. An attacker can put one on their own server to make that server look official. The certificate does not mean the server is safe. This is one part of a wider idea called staging capabilities, where an attacker prepares everything before the attack starts.
beginner.whyItMatters: Encrypted traffic is hard to read, so a certificate helps an attacker hide. A padlock in the browser makes people trust a fake login page. If your team only looks at certificate warnings, you may never see the attack traffic. Watching for new certificates using your brand names gives you an early warning.
howItWorks: The attacker needs a domain name, either bought new or taken over from someone else.
They request a certificate for that name from a free or paid certificate authority.
The authority checks the domain, then signs the certificate and returns it.
The attacker installs the certificate on their server and enables encrypted web traffic.
Visitors now see a padlock, and their browsers accept the connection without warning.
As an alternative, the attacker makes a self signed certificate, which browsers usually flag.
beginner.example: Imagine a night desk at a hospital where visitors sign in and receive a badge. The badge proves only that the front desk printed it, not that the wearer is a doctor. A stranger copies the badge design, prints one at home, and walks past every corridor check without a second look, because staff have stopped questioning anyone wearing a badge. A valid looking badge shows only that someone issued it. You still have to check who is wearing it, and why they are on the ward.
takeaways: A certificate proves identity to a computer, not honesty to a person.
Attackers use trusted certificates so their traffic looks like normal secure browsing.
Self signed certificates are still a warning sign worth investigating.

objectives: Explain what a TLS certificate does and why attackers want valid ones.
Describe the difference between a publicly trusted and a self signed certificate.
Identify certificate transparency logs as a source of early warning.
Explain why a padlock in a browser is not proof that a site is safe.
Summarise how a newly issued certificate for a lookalike domain can be detected.
